Anguish is a severe, intense form of emotional or mental pain — the kind that overwhelms a person so completely that it feels unbearable. It is not ordinary sadness or worry. It is what happens when pain cuts so deeply that a person feels crushed from the inside.

Think of it this way: if sadness is a bruise, anguish is a deep, open wound.

Anguish is the feeling a mother experiences when she learns her child has died. It is the feeling that grips a person when they watch someone they love suffer and can do absolutely nothing to help. It is the feeling that comes from carrying a guilt so heavy you feel it in your bones, knowing you cannot undo what was done.

The key qualities of anguish are:

Intensity — It sits at the extreme end of the scale of human suffering. This is not a word you use for mild discomfort or everyday sadness. It is reserved for some of the deepest pain a human being can feel.

An inner quality — Anguish comes from within. It lives in the mind, the heart, and the soul. You feel it, even when nothing visible is physically wrong with your body.

Overwhelm — A person in anguish is not just unhappy. They are consumed by the pain. It is hard to think, breathe, speak, or function normally.

Anguish is typically caused by situations involving deep loss, helplessness, or grief — and often all three at once. Common causes include the death of a beloved person, being forced to watch suffering you cannot stop, devastating guilt over something you've done or failed to do, a parent separated from their child, or finding yourself trapped in a situation with no way out and no hope. The common thread in all of these is that something deeply, fundamentally wrong has happened — something that cannot easily be fixed or forgotten.

While anguish is primarily an emotional and mental word, it can sometimes describe extreme physical pain — particularly when that pain is so severe it overwhelms a person's entire being, body and mind together. However, in everyday English, almost every use of the word refers to emotional or mental suffering. If you simply say "anguish" without any other context, people will assume you mean inner, emotional pain.

Anguish is so powerful that it rarely stays hidden. A person experiencing anguish might cry out or sob uncontrollably, tremble or collapse, go completely silent and still — frozen by the weight of what they're feeling — or be unable to eat, sleep, or carry out the simplest tasks. Their face often reflects it directly: twisted, pale, broken. This is why writers use anguish often — it is a visible, physical experience even though it originates emotionally.

This is the part most learners need most, and it's worth getting right.

Sadness is far lighter than anguish. You feel sadness when a friend cancels plans, when a favourite season ends, or when you miss home. Anguish is incomparably heavier and more extreme. Using anguish for small things would sound dramatic and wrong.

Grief is very close to anguish and is specifically tied to loss — especially the death of someone loved. Anguish is broader: you can feel anguish from guilt or helplessness, not just from loss. Anguish also tends to feel more acute and sharp in a given moment, while grief often describes a longer, sustained state of mourning.

Agony is anguish's closest twin, and the two are sometimes interchangeable. The subtle difference is that agony leans slightly more toward physical pain, while anguish leans slightly more toward emotional pain. You'd more naturally say "he was in agony from the broken bones" and "she felt anguish when she heard the news" — though both words can describe either type of pain, and both are extreme.

Distress is real suffering, but noticeably less extreme than anguish. A person in distress is troubled and struggling; a person in anguish is being torn apart inside. Distress is intense worry or hardship; anguish is devastation.

Torment involves repeated, ongoing suffering — often caused by something that won't stop, like relentless guilt or an abuser. Anguish can be a single, acute moment of pain. Torment tends to stretch across time; anguish can strike in an instant.

Misery is a duller, more prolonged state of unhappiness — it stretches on. Anguish is sharper and more acute, even if it can also last a long time.

As a noun, "anguish" is almost always uncountable, meaning you do not normally say "an anguish" or "two anguishes." You simply say "anguish" — it behaves like water or air, as a substance rather than a countable object.

However, you can use quantity expressions with it: "a moment of anguish," "a pang of anguish," "waves of anguish."

The most common pattern is "in anguish" — this is the phrase you will encounter most:

"She cried out in anguish when she heard the news."
"He buried his face in his hands in anguish."

Other natural patterns:

"His face was twisted with anguish."
"The loss filled her with anguish she couldn't describe."
"Years of mental anguish followed the accident." — "mental anguish" and "emotional anguish" are very common collocations that specify the type.
"He couldn't hide his anguish."
"The anguish of losing a child never fully leaves."

If you had to carry just one phrase with you to remember this word forever, it would be this: anguish is unbearable inner pain. It is what happens when suffering becomes so great that a person feels they cannot carry it — and yet, somehow, must.
